name: Mexoryl XL (drometrizole trisiloxane)

lead: Mexoryl XL is L'Oreal's broad-spectrum UV filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX in European and Asian sunscreens, and sought for long-term UV protection of facial skin. Less UV damage means slower photoaging and more even tone.

It is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived filter that absorbs UVB and UVA, with peaks near 303 and 344 nm. It is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not the US. Studies cited tested finished L'Oreal sunscreens containing it, not the filter alone.

paras: People find drometrizole trisiloxane on the ingredient lists of sunscreens sold outside the US and use them as daily facial or body protection, usually in combination formulas with ecamsule.
The sources reviewed contain no specific safety findings for this filter. It is not approved in the US.

angle.text: Mexoryl XL is L'Oreal's broad-spectrum filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX in sunscreens sold outside the US, and is sought for long-term UV protection of facial skin. Blocking UVA and UVB slows photoaging and keeps tone even.

lead: Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold by L'Oreal as Mexoryl XL, is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived UV filter that absorbs in both UVB and UVA, with peaks reported at 303 nm and 344 nm.[1] It is the ingredient in many European and Asian sunscreens that provides broad-spectrum protection, and it is often combined with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX), a pairing Wikipedia describes as synergistic.[1]

People seek out sunscreens containing it as part of daily sun protection, with the appearance goals of preventing sunburn, tanning-related darkening, uneven pigmentation and photoageing of the face. Dermatology reviews list it with other organic and inorganic filters when describing absorption properties and photostability of modern sunscreens.[2]

Wikipedia reports that sunscreens containing it are approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not in the United States.[1] A 2025 review of US sunscreen regulation describes it among newer filters available internationally and not in the US, attributing this to regulatory inertia and discussing a new FDA over-the-counter monograph process as a possible pathway.[3]

paras: The compound has formula C24H39N3O3Si3, a molar mass of about 502 g/mol, and is also called silatrizole.[1] Wikipedia describes it as a broad-spectrum UV absorber, lipophilic, with absorption peaks at 303 nm in the UVB range and 344 nm in the UVA range.[1] Its sister filter ecamsule (terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid, Mexoryl SX) is water-soluble, and the two are described as acting together.[1][2]

Drometrizole trisiloxane is an organic, oil-soluble filter. It absorbs ultraviolet photons in the skin-surface film and dissipates the energy rather than letting it reach living skin cells, with absorption peaks at 303 nm (UVB) and 344 nm (UVA) [1]. Because UVB drives sunburn and UVA contributes to tanning, pigmentation and photoageing, a filter that covers both ranges is the reason people look for products containing it [2].

Its sister filter ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) is water-soluble and absorbs UVA with a peak near 345 nm; Wikipedia's ecamsule article reports that the pair acts synergistically, protecting more than either alone, and that ecamsule is photostable, unlike avobenzone, which needs stabilizers [1][4]. A 2004 comparative study of UV-induced pigmentation protection reported a synergistic effect when Mexoryl XL was added to formulas containing Mexoryl SX [5].

The Mexoryl family was developed at L'Oreal. Wikipedia reports that L'Oreal patented ecamsule in 1982, that the EU approved it in 1991, and that sunscreens with it have been sold in Europe and Canada since 1993; the US FDA cleared ecamsule in 2006, but only for products registered under a New Drug Application rather than as a general sunscreen ingredient [4]. Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold as Mexoryl XL, was added to many European and Asian formulas as an oil-phase UVA/UVB filter and is also called silatrizole [1].

In the United States, sunscreen filters are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, and a 2025 review argued that the framework has kept newer filters, including drometrizole trisiloxane, from reaching US consumers, citing regulatory inertia and the possibility of a new monograph order request process [3]. The FDA's consumer sunscreen page lists bemotrizinol, another newer filter, among permitted active ingredients as of June 2026 [6].

Drometrizole trisiloxane is a cosmetic ingredient used as a UV filter in sunscreen products.[7] It is often listed in sunscreens alongside avobenzone (Parsol 1789), octocrylene and titanium dioxide in the formulations used in published studies.[8][5][9] Because the US FDA has not approved it, products containing it are mostly bought abroad or through importers by people who seek broad-spectrum European-style sunscreens.

Studies tested finished sunscreens rather than the filter alone. In a double-blind intraindividual study in 11 patients with photosensitive lupus erythematosus, three commercial sunscreens were tested against UVA plus UVB photoprovocation. The sunscreen containing Mexoryl SX, Mexoryl XL, avobenzone, octocrylene and titanium dioxide protected all 11 of 11 patients, while a comparison sunscreen with other filters protected 5 patients.[8] A 2004 comparative study measured protection against UV-induced pigmentation using an SPF-like method and found protection correlated with the concentration of Mexoryl SX and showed a synergistic effect when Mexoryl XL was added.[5]

A 2008 study describing a human in vivo method for studying melanocytic nevi tested a high-protection sunscreen containing octocrylene, Parsol 1789, titanium dioxide, Mexoryl SX and Mexoryl XL on nevi irradiated with UVB.[9] A 2008 dermatology review covers absorption properties, safety and photostability of filters including drometrizole trisiloxane.[2]

A 2026 risk assessment in Toxicological Research evaluated acute and repeated-dose toxicity, skin and eye irritation, sensitisation, reproductive and developmental toxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity and dermal absorption; its abstract reports oral and dermal LD50 values above 2 g/kg in rats.[7] The 2025 US regulatory review states that newer filters such as drometrizole trisiloxane have shown favourable safety and efficacy profiles internationally.[3]

Environmental studies have looked at organic UV filters in coastal waters; in one test of marine sediment microbes, no degradation of drometrizole trisiloxane was observed over the study period, whereas some other filters degraded.[10]

Sunscreens with the filter are approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan, and not in the United States.[1] The US review notes that the FDA's sunscreen framework, including GRASE criteria and maximal usage trials, has limited access to newer filters and that a new OTC monograph order request process may offer a way forward.[3]

People who seek out European-style broad-spectrum sunscreens look for Mexoryl XL on ingredient lists. Because the US has not approved the filter, sunscreens containing it are bought abroad or through importers [1][3]. Dermatology reviews describing sunscreen choice list filters by absorption spectrum and photostability rather than by brand [2]. The FDA's general advice is to use broad-spectrum products with an SPF of at least 15, and to check the label for broad-spectrum status [6].

Human studies found tested finished sunscreens that contained the filter among other ingredients, not the filter alone. In a double-blind intraindividual study of 11 patients with photosensitive lupus erythematosus, the sunscreen containing Mexoryl SX, Mexoryl XL, avobenzone, octocrylene and titanium dioxide protected all 11 against UVA plus UVB photoprovocation, while a comparison sunscreen protected 5 [8]. A 2004 study measured protection against UV-induced pigmentation and found it correlated with Mexoryl SX concentration and was boosted when Mexoryl XL was added [5]. A 2008 study developed a human in vivo method to study sunscreen effects on UVB-irradiated melanocytic nevi using a high-protection formula containing both Mexoryl filters [9].
No studies isolating Mexoryl XL as a single ingredient were found.
